paras: The East Baton Rouge church attack was an assault in April 1880 in which a crowd of white men went to a Black church in East Baton Rouge, Louisiana, drove away its occupants, closed the building and whipped some of its members. The attack is known only from a private letter by an unnamed Louisiana correspondent to J. E. Bruce, the Black editor of The Exodus in Washington, which reached Northern papers in late August 1880. Northern papers reprinted it as the letter-writer offered it, as evidence of what "Democratic rule" meant for Black Southerners ahead of the presidential election.

Bruce was described as "a colored man and Editor of The Exodus," a Washington paper that circulated chiefly among Black readers. His correspondent wrote to give "the political outlook from a colored man's point of view" and set the church attack first in a list of grievances that included the use of militia against striking plantation laborers, whippings in Jackson Parish, and emigration from Louisiana and Texas.

According to the letter, in April "a crowd of white roughs" went to a colored church in East Baton Rouge. The crowd drove away the people inside, closed the church and whipped some of the members. The letter named no church, victim or attacker, gave no day, and did not say what prompted the attack or how many people were whipped.
No report of arrests, an investigation or a reopening of the church appears in the coverage, and no Louisiana paper's account was found.

The New-York Tribune printed the letter on August 30 as a telegram from Washington under the headline "The Negro in the South" and the decks "Testimony of a Louisiana Colored Man" and "Whipped and Shot as in the Days of Slavery." The Chicago Daily Tribune ran the same text on September 2 under "Louisiana," and the Emporia News and Burlington Weekly Free Press carried it on September 10, the latter in abridged form. Where the New York and Chicago versions opened with the prospect for Black Louisianians being "glorious," the Kansas and Vermont versions read "gloomy."

On September 3 the New-York Tribune returned to the item in an editorial, "Southern Incidents," that quoted a shortened version alongside reports of duels and street violence. The editorial argued that "the customs of old slavery times" were reviving at the mere prospect of Southern power and asked what would follow if the South gained the White House. The Ellsworth American in Maine reprinted that editorial on September 16 with credit to the Tribune. No coverage in the Black press was found, and all the white papers that carried the story drew on the single letter rather than on any independent report.

accounts.label: Louisiana correspondent's letter to J. E. Bruce
accounts.gist: In April a crowd of white roughs went to a colored church in East Baton Rouge, drove away its occupants, closed the church and whipped some of the members; offered as one of several examples of what 'Democratic rule' meant for Black Louisianians.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune editorial
accounts.gist: Quotes a condensed version, 'a crowd of whites went to a colored church, drove away the occupants, whipped the members and closed the church', as evidence that slavery-era customs were reviving in the South.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headlined the letter 'The Negro in the South' with the deck 'Whipped and Shot as in the Days of Slavery' and printed the correspondent's partisan charges against Democratic rule without comment.
The Tribune's 'Southern Incidents' editorial used the church item, with sarcasm about Southern 'old times', to argue that the prospect of Democratic victory was reviving slavery-era practice.
Chicago, Emporia and Burlington papers reprinted the Washington letter, and the Ellsworth American reprinted the Tribune editorial, without added comment on the church attack.

conflicts.note: The editorial's wording is a condensed paraphrase of the letter; the letter as printed in A1 is the closer text.
